Chapter 1: Why Our View of the World Is Often Distorted
Have you ever wondered why our view of the world can sometimes feel a little off?
The way each of us sees things isn’t just shaped by what we’ve lived through. It’s influenced by what we hear in the news, the stories that grab our attention, and—maybe most of all—the mental shortcuts we use every day. These shortcuts, or instincts, help us make sense of all the information we get. But here’s the thing: they can seriously distort our picture of what’s really going on.
If you ask most people how the world is doing, they’ll usually paint a pretty grim picture. But the first step to seeing things clearly is realizing that our mental image of global progress is often stuck in the past—and way too negative.
Let’s talk about something called the “gap instinct.” You’ve probably heard it before—the idea that the world is split in two: rich versus poor, developed versus developing, lucky versus struggling. It’s like imagining a huge canyon with people on either side and nothing in between. But is that really how things are?
Actually, most people today live somewhere in the middle. Over the last few decades, health, income, and education have steadily improved for billions. The world isn’t divided into two frozen groups; it’s more like a spectrum, with lots of movement and progress.
So why do we hold onto this outdated idea? Well, think about how we get our information. News stories almost always focus on the big, dramatic stuff—disasters, conflicts, crises. And that makes sense—they grab our attention. But because of this, the slow, steady improvements—the good news—barely get noticed. Our minds are drawn to the exceptional and the alarming, which makes it really easy to believe that things are getting worse, even when the facts say otherwise.
So, what can you do about it? Next time you hear something shocking or upsetting, pause for a moment. Ask yourself: Is this story actually showing the full picture, or is it just focusing on the extremes? For instance, when you hear about poverty, don’t just think about the very poorest or the super-rich. Remember that most people are living somewhere in between.
Picture global income as a smooth curve, not two separate blocks. That small shift can totally reframe how you see the world.
Here are a few simple ways to beat the gap instinct:
Look for the majority in the middle—not just the extremes. Ask for data that shows the whole spread, not just the outliers. And remind yourself: most people’s lives aren’t as desperate or as glamorous as the most dramatic headlines make it seem.
When you start seeing things this way, the world opens up as a complex, dynamic place that’s actually getting better for most people. And that new perspective? It’s the best foundation you can have for building a truly fact-based view of the world.
